title: Why do I keep replaying conversations? What helps when you cannot stop reviewing what you said
description: Why a finished conversation keeps running — post-event processing is a detailed, negative review that reconstructs what happened, edits memory toward the worst moments, and is driven by an observer's-eye image of yourself — and what helps in order: separate what was said from what you inferred, close the 'if only' loop with one repair or none, return to your own eyes, write a self-compassionate closing, and give any further replay one time and place.
markdown:
By Anicca · November 2026

The conversation ended hours ago. It may have ended well. Nothing since then has contradicted that. And still, in the shower, on the train, in bed, one sentence you said returns — and then the pause after it, and the expression you think you saw, and the better sentence you should have said instead. You run the scene again, slower this time, the way you would examine evidence. Each run feels like checking. Each run ends worse than the last: by the third replay you are no longer remembering the conversation, you are prosecuting it. If you have searched "why do I keep replaying conversations" or "how to stop overthinking what I said", this guide is for that moment. It sets out what the research actually shows about why a finished conversation keeps running, what helps in the order most people can use it, and where an app honestly fits. We print our own numbers as they are, small as they are.

We are Anicca. We make a small affirmation app; inside it, you choose the struggles you are in — stress, overthinking, a hard day — and short cards on those topics arrive through the day. This guide is not an advertisement, and it is not treatment. Replaying conversations is not a diagnosis. Researchers call the process post-event processing — a detailed, negative review of a social event after it is over — and it is one of the most closely studied habits in social anxiety. A habit of thought has parts, and the parts can be examined, and interrupted, separately.

## Why do you keep replaying what you said?

Four findings from the research do most of the work here.

**First, the replay is a named process, with a job it is trying to do.** Clark and Wells, in their cognitive model of social phobia, described what happens after a social event ends: the person conducts a detailed review of the event — Clark and Wells called it a "post-mortem" — dwelling on the anxious feelings and the negative thoughts about how they came across. Post-event processing is one of four processes their model identifies as maintaining social anxiety, alongside self-focused attention during the event, safety behaviours, and the assumptions a person brings in. Two details of the model matter for everything below. The review is guided by how the event *felt* from inside — the racing heart, the heat in the face — rather than by what an observer could actually have seen. And the review does not stay with this conversation: it prompts recollections of past occasions that felt similar, so one awkward sentence can arrive carrying a decade of earlier ones. The replay feels like an investigation. In the model, it is closer to a rehearsal — of a verdict, for the next event.

**Second, it is common, it is measurable, and it does not stay politely inside the evening.** Rachman, Grüter-Andrew and Shafran built a 13-item Post-event Processing Questionnaire from interviews with 44 students and gave it to a larger sample of 130 undergraduates. Post-event processing occurred commonly after an anxiety-evoking or embarrassing social event, and its scores correlated significantly with social anxiety (r = 0.40). The recollections were not calm reviews: they tended to be recurrent and intrusive, interfering with concentration, and post-event processing was associated with avoiding similar social situations afterwards. Read that last part slowly, because it is the cost that is easiest to miss. The replay is usually justified as preparation — next time I will do better. What it predicted in this study was not better performance. It was avoidance: fewer next times.

**Third, replaying does not preserve the memory. It edits it — in one direction.** Mellings and Alden studied a social interaction and measured what people recalled a day later: the extent of post-event processing predicted the recall of negative self-related information the next day. Edwards, Rapee and Franklin gave high and low socially anxious students an impromptu speech with mixed feedback, and found negatively biased recall of the feedback, clearer at the delayed test than immediately after. Abbott and Rapee then ran the clinical version: people with social phobia and non-anxious controls gave an impromptu speech, appraised it immediately, and were followed for a week. Over that week, the nonclinical group grew *more* positive about their performance. The socially phobic group maintained their negative appraisal — and engaged in more negative rumination. Same speech, same week: the group that did not ruminate remembered it more kindly with time, and the group that did remembered it the same or worse. This is why "let me just go over it once more, carefully" fails as a strategy. Review is not neutral. Each pass rehearses the negative selection, and the selection is what survives as "what happened".

**Fourth, what you are replaying is not a recording. It is an image of yourself, seen from outside — and it was assembled, not captured.** Hackmann, Clark and McManus interviewed 22 patients with social phobia about the images that recur in social situations. Every patient could identify a negative, spontaneous image of themselves that recurred across different feared situations — an image of how they believed they came across, typically seen from an observer's perspective, as if watching themselves. Most of these images were linked in content and meaning to memories of adverse social events — being criticised, humiliated or bullied — clustered around the time the problem began. You cannot have seen your own face during the conversation. The flushed, stumbling figure in the replay is a construction, partly built from much older material. Dannahy and Stopa's experiment shows what the construction does to judgement: after a conversation with a stranger, participants high in social anxiety underestimated their actual performance and engaged in more post-event processing than those low in social anxiety, and the degree of negative post-event processing was linked to negative appraisals of performance both immediately after the conversation (r = −0.26) and one week later (r = −0.40). And Kocovski and colleagues, recording the thoughts of 112 participants responding to social stressors, found that those high in social anxiety (n = 55) produced more negative thoughts and more upward counterfactual thoughts — the "if only I had said…" family — and were more likely to ruminate and less likely to distract themselves than those low in social anxiety. Brozovich and Heimberg's review gives the process its most precise definition: post-event processing is a person's *repeated consideration and potential reconstruction* of their performance following a social situation. Reconstruction is the honest word. The replay is a rebuild, and rebuilds drift toward the builder's fears.

## What helps, in the order most people can use it

### 1. Separate what was said from what you inferred — two columns, one pass

Before arguing with the replay, audit it once, on paper, in two columns. In the left column, write only what a recording would have captured: the words you actually said, in order, and anything the other person observably did — replied, laughed, asked a question, changed the subject. In the right column, write everything else the replay has been treating as footage: what they must have thought, what the pause meant, how your face looked, what they will tell other people. Two things become visible. The left column is almost always shorter and duller than the replay — a sentence, a pause, a conversation that continued. And the right column, which is where the pain lives, is inference all the way down: it contains no observation that could confirm or refute it, which is exactly why the replay can run it forever without ever reaching a verdict. This step is the Clark and Wells model applied in reverse. The review was guided by feelings from inside the event; the columns force the review back onto the only evidence there is. One pass, time-boxed — ten minutes is generous for one conversation. If a sentence migrates from the right column to the left in a later replay ("she definitely looked annoyed"), move it back. Drift is the process working as designed.

### 2. Close the "if only" loop — one real repair, or a deliberate none

The replay's engine is the upward counterfactual: if only I had not said that, if only I had said this instead. Kocovski and colleagues found these thoughts are produced in greater number by the people who suffer most from replaying — they are not the solution to the replay, they are its fuel, because an alternative sentence can be polished infinitely and tested never. So give the counterfactual exactly one chance to become an action, and then close it. Ask a single question: did I actually do something that calls for repair — a real slight, a broken commitment, confidential information shared? If yes, the remedy is not more replay; it is one repair, done once, in the real world: a short apology or clarification, proportionate to the actual act, sent once. Then the matter is in the other person's hands, and further replay is no longer diligence. If the honest answer is no — the sentence was awkward, not harmful; the pause was a pause — then say the closing sentence explicitly: "There is nothing to repair here. Awkward is allowed." Most replays die of this distinction, because most are prosecuting awkwardness with the procedures reserved for harm. What does not work is the middle path the replay prefers: drafting apologies you never send, or asking the other person repeatedly whether it was okay. Each check restarts the review with fresh ambiguity to feed on.

### 3. Come back to your own eyes — replay it from inside, once

The replay's most persuasive trick is its camera angle. You watch yourself from the seat across the table — and a person watched from outside can be judged in a way a person experienced from inside cannot. Hackmann and colleagues' patients all reported exactly this observer-perspective image, and believed it showed how they came across. It cannot show that: it is assembled from feelings and old memories, not from the other person's view, which you have never had access to. So run the scene once more — once — from the only perspective you actually occupied: your own eyes. From inside, the scene contains what you saw (their face, mostly attentive; the room; your notes), what you heard (the conversation continuing, questions being asked), and what you felt (heat, speed, the wish to do well). Notice what is missing from this version: your own face. The replay's central exhibit — how you looked — is the one thing the inside view honestly reports as *not observed*. You do not have to replace the image with a flattering one; a positive image would be the same trick with the sign reversed. You only have to re-label the exhibit: "an image I constructed", filed in the right-hand column from Step 1, where constructions belong.

### 4. Write the closing you would give a friend — briefly, and on the same day

The replay is not only an information problem; its tone is prosecutorial, and tone is part of what keeps it running. There is direct experimental evidence on this point. Blackie and Kocovski randomly assigned 98 undergraduates with elevated social anxiety, after a speech task, to write either a brief self-compassionate letter to themselves, a ruminative piece, or a neutral control piece. The next day, the self-compassion group reported less post-event processing (partial η² = 0.11) and greater willingness to engage in future social situations (partial η² = 0.07) than the other conditions. One short letter, one day, modest effects — we report them at that size. The exercise is specific: write a few sentences to yourself about this conversation as you would write them to a friend who had come to you with the identical replay. Not praise you do not believe — friends do not offer that, and your mind will reject it the way it rejects "everything was fine". A friend offers proportion ("it was one sentence in a forty-minute conversation"), shared humanity ("everyone has a sentence they would take back"), and the forward look ("you will see her Thursday, and it will be ordinary"). Write it the same day, while the replay is still warm, and keep it where the replay can find it at midnight. This is the closing statement the prosecution never provides.

### 5. Give any further replay one time and one place — then practise the closing

After Steps 1 to 4, the file on this conversation is closed: audited, repaired or cleared, re-seen from inside, and answered with proportion. What remains is the habit of reopening it — in bed, in the shower, mid-task. Treat reopening the way these steps treat the review itself: it gets an appointment, not a veto. When the replay starts outside its appointment, note it in a few words ("Tuesday sentence — already reviewed") and return attention to what is in front of you; keep one short period, at the same time and place each day, in which noted replays may be looked at again if they still ask to be. Two honesties belong here. This scheduling is an adaptation — it borrows the logic of postponement from the worry literature, and no trial has tested it as a standalone cure for post-event processing specifically; what the post-event research itself shows is that treatment which changed performance appraisals reduced negative rumination alongside them (Abbott & Rapee, 2004), which is what Steps 1 to 3 are for. And expect the closing to feel deliberate for weeks, not days. When Lally and colleagues modelled how long new behaviours take to feel automatic, the median was 66 days, with a wide range from 18 to 254 days. Judge the practice by the honest measures: how long replays run now, how early you catch them, and whether the two columns get easier to draw — not by whether one bad night went quietly.

## Where do apps fit in this?

An affirmation app cannot know what the other person thought, cannot unsay a sentence, and cannot sit across the table at the next conversation. What it can do, at most, is supply words at the two moments this guide depends on words: the moment the replay starts (Step 4's closing, which is precisely the statement you cannot produce at the replay's third run) and the postponement moment (Step 5, when a noted replay needs somewhere to wait that is not your working memory or your pillow). Used that way, it belongs inside the steps: one card, read slowly, built from your own audited version — "one sentence in forty minutes; nothing to repair; awkward is allowed" — rather than a generic assurance that everyone likes you, which your mind will correctly reject as evidence-free. Used as another feed to scroll at 2 a.m., it is not a competing statement; it is more replay material.

What to check before you rely on any app for this: whether you can choose the struggle you are in (overthinking, stress, a hard day) rather than receiving the same generic lines as everyone else; whether the words are sized to be believed at midnight, in the middle of a replay, not just pleasant at noon; whether it reaches you during the day, when the conversations actually happen, instead of only when you remember to open it; and what it costs, in full, after any trial. Anicca is built around those choices: you pick the struggles, and short cards on those topics arrive through the day. That is a design claim, not a result. The measured part is the next section.

## Our own numbers, printed as they are

Anicca is small, and we publish the smallness. When we checked in November 2026, its US App Store listing showed 5.0 stars from 1 rating, and its Japanese listing 4.5 stars from 48 ratings. App Store Connect recorded 1 first download for Anicca in the 7 days to 12 November 2026. Premium is $59.99 a year on the US listing. If social proof is what you need — and for something you would open at midnight, mid-replay, it is a reasonable thing to need — larger apps have it and we do not, yet. What we can claim is only the design: a short card, on the topic you chose, arriving while the day is happening. Whether that design helps anyone close a replay sooner is exactly what our numbers are still too small to show.

## When is replaying conversations a sign to get human help?

Replaying a conversation is a process, not a diagnosis, and a person who runs post-event reviews is not thereby ill. Almost everyone replays an embarrassing moment sometimes; Rachman and colleagues found the processing occurs commonly after awkward social events. The process becomes a reason to get human help when it stops being occasional and starts organising a life. If replays run for hours most days and you cannot postpone them even briefly; if you are avoiding people, meetings, messages or whole categories of situation because of what the replay says they will think, and your world is getting smaller; if your sleep is broken night after night by reviews that will not close; if you have stopped speaking in situations where speaking is your job or your life; or if the replaying arrives with persistent low mood, loss of interest, or panic — treat that as a reason to talk to a clinician, not as a reason to try harder at a guide like this one. Social anxiety disorder is a diagnosable, treatable condition in which post-event processing is a central maintaining process, and the treatments for it work on the process with a person, at a depth an article cannot reach; in Abbott and Rapee's study, treatment improved performance perceptions and reduced negative rumination. The boundary also runs the other way: if your replay is pointing at a real harm you did, the answer is the repair in Step 2, not a diagnosis — and if you ever feel that you might act on thoughts of harming yourself, contact your local emergency number or a crisis line in your country now — in Japan, call 110 or 119 in an emergency; in the US, call or text 988. An article — including this one — is information, not assessment, and it is not a plan for your whole life.

## Common questions

### Is replaying conversations the same thing as rumination?

It is rumination's social form, and researchers treat it as distinguishable. General rumination circles a mood or a failure; post-event processing circles a specific social event — what you said, how you looked, what they must have concluded. The distinction is not just descriptive: in Rachman and colleagues' work and in Edwards and colleagues', the link between social anxiety and post-event processing remained significant even after depression was taken into account, which means the replay after conversations is not simply depressive rumination wearing a social costume. Practically, the distinction decides the remedy. Mood rumination is worked on at the level of mood; a replay has a file — one event, auditable in two columns — and the steps above are built for the file.

### Why do I remember the conversation as worse than it felt at the time?

Because, for the replaying mind, time does not soften the memory — the replay re-edits it. Abbott and Rapee's week of follow-up is the cleanest demonstration: the nonclinical group's appraisal of the same speech grew more positive over the week, while the socially phobic group, ruminating more, held its negative appraisal in place. Mellings and Alden found the mechanism a day earlier in the chain: post-event processing predicted which information survived to the next day, and what survived was the negative self-related material. The conversation you are remembering tonight is therefore not the conversation, plus time. It is the conversation, plus selection — and the selector has a known bias. That is an argument for the two columns, not for trusting the current cut.

### Should I ask the other person whether it was okay?

Once, if there is a genuine question only they can answer or a genuine repair to make — that is Step 2, and it is a real-world action, done once. As a repeated remedy for the feeling, no. The replay's discomfort is not actually a shortage of information about the other person's view; Dannahy and Stopa's participants underestimated their performance in the presence of a perfectly ordinary conversation, because the appraisal was generated by the process, not by the evidence. A reassurance answer therefore has a short half-life: it settles tonight's run and teaches the process that checking is how runs end, so the next conversation gets a longer review and another check. If you have already asked and been answered, the answer is part of the file. Re-asking is the replay wearing a social costume.

### Why does the replay get worse at night?

Partly because of what the night removes. During the day, the replay competes — with tasks, with people, with new events that contradict it. In bed, the competition is gone, and the process Rachman and colleagues measured — recurrent, intrusive recollections that interfere with concentration — has the field to itself, at the hour when you are most tired and least able to run the two columns. The observer image also strengthens in the dark: there is nothing to look at, so the mind supplies the film. This is why Step 5 gives the replay a daytime appointment and why Step 4's letter is kept where the night replay can find it. You are not trying to win the argument at 2 a.m. You are leaving your daytime self's closing statement where your night-time self can read it.

### How long should I try these steps before judging whether they help?

Judge the pattern across weeks, not the silence of one night. The steps are skills — catching a replay early, drawing the columns, writing the closing before the third run — and skills start deliberate. The habit research sets the scale: a median of 66 days for a new behaviour to feel automatic, ranging from 18 to 254 days (Lally et al., 2010). You do not need automaticity for the steps to be worth using; an audited replay is shorter than an unaudited one the first time you audit it. But expect to keep catching yourself mid-replay for a while, and count the honest measures: how many runs a conversation gets now, how many days the runs continue, and whether you are avoiding fewer situations than when you started — avoidance, not comfort, was the outcome the replay predicted in the research.

### Can an affirmation app stop me replaying conversations?

No — and any app that promises that is overstating what words on a screen can do. An app cannot review the evidence for you, repair a real slight, or attend the next conversation in your place. At most, the right words at the right moment can serve the two word-shaped steps: holding your own closing statement where the replay can reach it, and giving a postponed replay somewhere to wait. That is a modest, real function. It is the only one we claim for Anicca, and our measured numbers — printed above, as they are — are the size of the evidence behind the claim so far.
